prompt: Ice cream sales and sunburns go together, but ice cream doesn't cause sunburn.
tells: Ice cream sales and sunburns go together
why: Both rise in hot, sunny weather. Going together isn't causing.
trap: Sun is the other explanation, but the lesson is correlation vs cause.

prompt: Students who drink coffee get better grades, so the school considers giving everyone coffee.
tells: so the school considers giving everyone coffee
why: Maybe hard workers drink coffee. The link doesn't show coffee causes grades.
trap: Testing small would help, but the error is assuming cause.

prompt: People who use the app's budgeting feature save more, so the team says the feature makes people save.
tells: so the team says the feature makes people save
why: Savers may simply choose budgeting tools. The link isn't proof of cause.
trap: Other explanations exist, but the clue is jumping from link to cause.

prompt: Towns with more firefighters have more fires, because bigger towns have more of both.
tells: bigger towns have more of both
why: A third thing (size) drives both. That's correlation, not cause.
trap: Base rates are about frequency; this is a hidden third factor.

prompt: To check, they randomly give the feature to half the users and compare.
tells: randomly give the feature to half the users
why: A random split is how you test cause rather than just link.
trap: It's small and tests a claim, but its purpose is cause vs correlation.

prompt: Sales rose the week the new logo launched, so they credit the logo.
why: Happening at the same time isn't proof of cause.
trap: Other reasons are the follow-up; the trap is cause from timing.
